passage: Usha, you're sighing about your father's grumbling, so let me tell you about my Bade Papa. When I was twenty-four, I lived with him in Indore for a year while I worked at the bank. So he asked, 'What would you have done with that job, Dada?' Dada stopped mid-grievance and, slowly, talked about building schools. Later, on the bench, Irfan said quietly to Tenzin, 'I never want to be seventy and still counting who wronged me.' Tenzin nodded. 'Then don't start counting now.'

passage: Thomas, you say you're bored of your job and everything is fine. Let me tell you about me at twenty-five, in the railway accounts office in Madras. The next month I started teaching accounts free on Sunday mornings to boys from the railway colony who couldn't afford tuition. Forty years later, three of those boys are chartered accountants. Now, sitting in the dark, he tried to think of one thing he was building that wasn't for himself. Nothing came. At ten his flatmate Mridul came in with a torch, sweaty and grinning, back from the blood bank where he volunteered on Thursdays. 'Fourteen donors tonight,' Mridul said. Tejas said, 'Nice,' and felt something sink. He wasn't a bad person. He had just stopped looking outward. 'Can I come next Thursday?' he asked.

qa.q: Where does Mridul volunteer on Thursdays?
qa.a: At the blood bank.

qa.q: What did Tejas feel when Mridul said 'Fourteen donors tonight'?
qa.a: Tejas felt something sink, a flat, empty feeling at realising he was building nothing beyond himself.

qa.q: What did Tejas do right at the end of the evening?
qa.a: He asked to join Mridul next Thursday, taking a first small step outward instead of just feeling bad.

qa.q: How might Mridul react to Tejas asking to come?
qa.a: Mridul would probably be pleased and welcoming, glad to share something that clearly lifts his own evenings.

grounding: During a power cut a comfortable young worker realises his life has turned entirely inward and feels flat.

passage:
March: Vidya spent her lunch hours teaching Gargi, the new junior at the Pune design studio, everything she had learned about typography the hard way. She showed her the mistakes too.
June: at the big client presentation, the client loved the logo. It had started as Vidya's rough sketch, but Gargi had reworked it completely. When the client asked who designed it, Vidya said at once, 'Gargi did. It's her work.' Gargi stared at her, stunned.
November: the studio head offered Gargi the lead on the new museum project, the one Vidya had hoped for. Vidya felt the sting clearly, went for a long walk, and came back. She stopped at Gargi's desk. 'You'll be brilliant. If you want a second pair of eyes, I'm here. If you don't, that's fine too.' Gargi hugged her, and Vidya found she meant every word.

qa.q: What did Vidya say when the client asked who designed the logo?
qa.a: 'Gargi did. It's her work.'

qa.q: How did Vidya feel when Gargi got the museum project?
qa.a: Vidya felt a clear sting of disappointment, then, after a long walk, genuine happiness for Gargi.

qa.q: What makes Vidya's mentoring free of ego?
qa.a: She shared her mistakes, credited Gargi publicly, and offered help without insisting once Gargi outgrew her.

qa.q: How might Gargi feel about Vidya after November?
qa.a: Gargi likely feels grateful and deeply supported, which is why she hugs her.

grounding: Over months a young designer teaches a junior, credits her publicly and accepts being outgrown.

passage: Kamal, you're worried the new boy you're training will overtake you. Let me tell you about Harpreet. I was twenty-five, a sub-editor at the Chandigarh paper, and they gave me this nervous kid straight from journalism school. I taught him everything: how to cut a story without killing it, how to call a source back. His first front-page piece was half my rewrite, but I put only his name on it. Four years later, he became my boss. My boss! I sulked for exactly one evening. Then I went in the next morning and said, 'Congratulations, Harpreet. Don't forget to cut the adjectives.' He laughed. He still sends me his big stories before print: 'Gurleen Didi, read this first.' That's the best thing I ever grew, beta. It wasn't mine to keep.

qa.q: Where did Gurleen work at twenty-five?
qa.a: As a sub-editor at the Chandigarh paper.

qa.q: How did Gurleen feel when Harpreet became her boss?
qa.a: She felt hurt and sulky for one evening before choosing to be generous.

qa.q: Gurleen put only Harpreet's name on his first front-page piece. Why was that a good choice?
qa.a: It gave him the confidence of owning the work and showed she cared about his growth more than her own credit.

qa.q: How might Harpreet feel about Gurleen now?
qa.a: Harpreet clearly trusts and respects her, still sending his big stories to her first.

grounding: A senior journalist recalls mentoring a junior who later became her boss, giving credit and accepting being outgrown.

passage: The demo for the hospital client was at ten, and at eight the office internet went down. Chinmay, who had built the appointment app's first version, could have taken over and patched it himself; he knew the code best. Instead he turned to Vandana, the junior he had been coaching for six months. 'You rewrote the booking module. You know it better than me now. What do we need?' She blinked, then rattled off a plan: run it locally, use her phone hotspot, skip the payments screen. It worked. In the meeting, when the client praised the booking flow, Chinmay said, 'That's Vandana's design. She'll walk you through it.' Afterwards his manager said, 'You could have presented it yourself.' Chinmay shrugged. 'She's going to be better than me. I'd like to have helped with that.'

qa.q: What went down at eight?
qa.a: The office internet.

qa.q: What does Chinmay's shrug suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests Chinmay felt calm and content, proud of Vandana rather than anxious about being outgrown.

qa.q: Why was asking Vandana for the plan a good choice under pressure?
qa.a: She knew the booking module best, so letting her lead solved the problem and gave her the chance to show her skill.

qa.q: How might Vandana feel when Chinmay credits her in front of the client?
qa.a: Vandana would likely feel proud and trusted, seen for her own work instead of hidden behind her mentor.

grounding: Under a deadline a young developer lets his junior lead, credits her publicly and welcomes being outgrown.

passage: You asked if I feel like an adult. Honestly? Depends on the hour. I'm Pradeep, twenty-one. At 9 am I'm negotiating with my landlord in Hyderabad about the leaking tap, very serious, very grown-up. At 2 pm my father sends money for the rent and I feel about twelve. I choose my own courses, cook my own terrible dal, decide when I sleep. But when I got a fever last month, the first thing I did was call my mother and cry. My friend Vishal has a job already and pays for everything himself, and next to him I feel like I'm pretending. Then again, Vishal still sends his laundry home. Maybe nobody our age feels finished. I used to think this in-between feeling meant I was failing at growing up. Now I think it's just where I am.

qa.q: What does Pradeep negotiate with the landlord about?
qa.a: The leaking tap.

qa.q: How does Pradeep feel when the rent money arrives?
qa.a: Pradeep feels small and childish, about twelve, despite handling so much alone.

qa.q: What shift in thinking helps Pradeep?
qa.a: Seeing the in-between feeling as a normal stage rather than a failure, which eases the comparison with Vishal.

qa.q: How might Vishal see his own situation?
qa.a: Vishal may feel more independent with a job, yet still relies on home for laundry, so he may feel in-between too.

grounding: A young adult describes feeling neither child nor adult, partly dependent and partly independent, and sees it as normal.

passage:
Monday: Gargi signed her first rental agreement for a shared flat in Bengaluru, alone, reading every clause twice. She felt tall.
Thursday: her card was declined at the grocery shop; the month's money from home hadn't come yet. She put back the paneer, called Papa, and heard herself say sorry three times. She felt small, like a schoolgirl who'd lost her bus pass.
The next Sunday: on a video call, her older sister Sarika asked, 'So, are you a proper adult now?' Gargi laughed, then didn't. 'I don't know. Some days yes. Some days I want Mummy to tell me what to eat.' Sarika smiled. 'I'm twenty-six and I still call Mummy about dal. It doesn't mean you're failing.' Gargi hung up and cooked the dal badly, her own way.

qa.q: What did Gargi put back at the grocery shop?
qa.a: The paneer.

qa.q: How did Gargi feel when her card was declined?
qa.a: Gargi felt small and embarrassed, like a schoolgirl who'd lost her bus pass.

qa.q: What could help Gargi feel steadier about being in-between?
qa.a: Talking honestly with people like Sarika, and noticing both the grown-up things she handles and the help she still needs, without shame.

qa.q: How does Sarika see Gargi's worry?
qa.a: Sarika sees it as normal, sharing that at twenty-six she still calls Mummy about dal.

grounding: Across a week a young woman swings between feeling grown-up and childlike, and her sister reassures her it is common.

passage: Ayesha, you said you feel like a fake grown-up. Sit, and let your Avni Phuphi tell you about 1998. I was twenty-one, working my first job at a Delhi call centre, living in a working women's hostel. I paid my own rent and felt so independent. But every Sunday my father sent a parcel of food and an envelope of money, and I took it every time. One evening my roommate, Shabnam, found me crying over my first salary slip because it was less than Abbu earned when I was born. 'Are we adults or not?' I asked her. She laughed. 'We're both. Eat your parcel.' I decided then to stop asking. Three years later I tried to pay Abbu back for the envelopes. He tore up the cheque, and we both cried.

qa.q: Where did Avni live at twenty-one?
qa.a: In a working women's hostel in Delhi.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling crying over the first salary slip?
qa.a: Avni felt small and confused, comparing her pay to her father's and unsure whether she was really grown up.

qa.q: Avni decided to stop asking whether she was an adult yet. Why did that help?
qa.a: It let her accept being both independent and still supported, instead of feeling like a failure in between.

qa.q: How might Abbu have felt tearing up the cheque?
qa.a: Abbu probably felt proud and touched, and wanted Avni to know his help was never a debt.

grounding: An aunt recalls feeling half-independent and half-supported at twenty-one and learning that the in-between is normal.

passage: Yamini had until midnight to accept one of three offers: a design job in Bengaluru, a fellowship teaching in rural Odisha, or a master's seat in Pune. At nine her laptop charger died, and the corner cafe was closing at ten. She sat at the last table with her phone at twelve per cent, three tabs open, heart racing. Each one looked like a different life. Each one meant losing the other two. She texted Yusuf: 'what if i pick wrong and regret it forever.' He replied: 'what if all three are good and you're just choosing a flavour.' Yamini laughed, then stopped comparing salaries and asked herself one question: which one did she want to wake up to next Monday? At 9:52, with four per cent left, she accepted the fellowship, and felt terrified and light at once.

qa.q: What were Yamini's three offers?
qa.a: A design job in Bengaluru, a fellowship teaching in rural Odisha, and a master's seat in Pune.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling at the cafe table?
qa.a: Yamini felt excited but anxious, heart racing, afraid of picking wrong and regretting it forever.

qa.q: What question helped Yamini break the freeze?
qa.a: Which one she wanted to wake up to next Monday, which cut through endless comparison of salaries.

qa.q: How does Yusuf see Yamini's dilemma?
qa.a: Yusuf sees it lightly, as choosing between three good flavours rather than risking a wrong life.

grounding: Under a deadline a graduate with three open futures feels thrill and dread and breaks the freeze with one simple question.

passage: Every night in her Mumbai hostel room, Nirmala did the same thing: opened her college batch's photos and compared. Priyanka at a startup in Berlin. Faisal doing a PhD in Chennai. Someone engaged, someone backpacking. Nirmala had graduated in May and still hadn't applied anywhere. Every door looked open, and that was the problem. If she chose one, the others would close, and what if she chose the dull one? Her brother Suraj came to visit on Sunday and found her with twelve job tabs open and none filled in. 'You're shopping, not choosing,' he said, closing the laptop. 'Pick two. Apply. You can change later.' Nirmala felt a flash of annoyance, then relief. That night she applied to two jobs and stopped looking at the batch photos.

qa.q: How many job tabs did Nirmala have open?
qa.a: Twelve job tabs, none filled in.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling while comparing her batch's photos?
qa.a: Nirmala felt restless and anxious, excited by open doors but dreading choosing the dull one.

qa.q: Why was Suraj's advice to pick two a helpful one?
qa.a: It broke the freeze by making the choice small and reversible, stopping the endless comparison.

qa.q: How might Suraj see his sister's situation?
qa.a: Suraj sees her as stuck shopping rather than choosing, and wants to help her move.

grounding: A graduate facing endless options freezes and compares herself with others until her brother nudges her to choose.

passage:
'So Nikhil's moving to Delhi and wants me to come,' Rekha said, lying on Swati's bed.
'And?'
'And Kochi has that museum job. And my cousin says Bengaluru is where everything happens. And I'm twenty-two. What if I choose a city because of a boy and it's the wrong boy? What if I stay and miss the right one?'
'You're doing the thing again.'
'What thing?'
'Imagining ten futures and living in none.' Swati sat up. 'Which one makes you excited, not just not-scared?'
Rekha was quiet a long time. 'The museum. Honestly. And Nikhil... I'd visit.'
'Then that's a start.'
'But what if—'
'Rekha. Every choice closes doors. That's what makes it a choice.'
Rekha pulled the pillow over her face and laughed into it. 'I hate that you're right.'

qa.q: Where is Nikhil moving?
qa.a: To Delhi.

qa.q: What is Rekha feeling as she lists the options?
qa.a: Rekha feels excited by the options but anxious and frozen, afraid of choosing the wrong city or the wrong person.

qa.q: What question from Swati helps, and why?
qa.a: 'Which one makes you excited, not just not-scared?' It shifts Rekha from avoiding regret to noticing what she actually wants.

qa.q: How does Swati see Rekha's habit?
qa.a: Swati sees it as imagining ten futures and living in none, and gently pushes Rekha to accept that choosing means closing doors.

grounding: A young graduate weighing cities, jobs and a partner feels excitement and dread until a friend helps her notice what she wants.
